lines.narration: Up on the footbridge over the crossing, Sean asks Han how he ended up over here. Han answers sideways, the way he answers everything. You know those old westerns, where the cowboys make a run for the border? This is my Mexico.

Why didn't you let me race your car, Sean asks — you knew I'd wreck it. Because there's a lot of money, Han says, and I have money. One car for knowing what a man's made of is a prize he can live with. Look at those people down there, following the rules, letting fear lead them. The closest Han gets to a creed.
What happens if I don't, Sean asks. Han gives him the only rule he lives by. Life's simple — you make choices and you don't look back. So what do you drift for, then? You really wanna know? Let's go.

The RX-7 swings in beside the Skyline and the two cars orbit each other inside a cloud of their own smoke, the women laughing out the back window. No finish line, no money, no crowd. That is the answer.
Next morning, one instruction: out here you drift by feeling. So feel it. Sean runs the clifftop hairpin again and again, sawing at the wheel — and every run shreds a set of tyres he cannot pay for.

claim.subject: the friend in the pink hoodie

lines.narration: He funds the rubber the only way he can. Down a packed street he and Twinkie hawk goods to strangers — I'm so good, man, I can sell rubbers to a monk — and walk off thumbing a roll of cash.

claim.subject: the young man in the red beanie

lines.narration: Meanwhile Boswell has no idea. Sean's father lets himself into the flat, hits the light, finds dark rooms and a bed nobody has slept in. His face hardens from searching to certainty. The boy has not been coming home.
At the garage rail, Reiko leans in beside Han and tells him he has a visitor waiting below.

claim.subject: the woman in the satin dress

lines.narration: Han lets him off the leash. The two run door to door off the mountain road, onto the expressway, down through a parking deck, until the neon-plaza crowd swarms Sean's car. He grins through the reaching hands. The frightened look is gone.
Daylight, a classroom, a chat window on Neela's laptop: bama boy, how come i never c u drift. She reads it, smiles to herself, and hits enter.

That night they eat vending-machine food under an overpass, and the guard drops away. He calls himself a cool guy; she stops him cold — she hates that word, it is what the kids called her. Outsider, he says, can mean a lot of things.

Then she gives him the whole thing. Her mother came from Australia and worked a hostess bar; she died when Neela was ten; and the grandmother who took her in was DK's. The family that saved her is the one that owns her now.

She drives him up the hairpins, telling him she has been sneaking up here since before she had a licence, cutting class to watch the older kids drift. It was different back then, she says. Nobody bothered them. And the mood breaks open into laughter.

Then Morimoto, DK's enforcer, strides across the lot and puts Sean face down on the concrete with one swing — and Han, and the whole crew, just watch. Sean lifts his split face and glares back instead of staying down. Brave. Also the instinct that got him shipped out of Alabama.

claim.subject: the heavyset man in the tank top

lines.narration: Neela kneels beside him as the crew files out, and Han's warning lands on the kid's recklessness: he didn't just play with fire, he soaked the matches in gasoline. Pushed Neela and DK far past where Han can pull him back.

claim.subject: the man in the hooded jacket

lines.narration: So Neela does something worse. Still in her school uniform, she walks into DK's club, stops in the doorway where he lounges between two hostesses, and says three words to his face, in front of his men. You've changed, DK.

He reaches for the thing that will land: your mother was the best trick in all of Kabukicho, back in the day. Leave my mother out of this, she tells him. He keeps going, backs her against the wall, asks who would look twice at her if not for her uncle — until she stops answering and a tear runs down her cheek. He never raises his voice.
